report:
## Report

The claim that dark chocolate lowers stroke risk is not simply "false," but the evidence is weaker and more mixed than headlines suggest—so skepticism is reasonable, though outright denial goes too far.

**What the evidence shows:** A meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies found that higher chocolate consumption was associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease, including stroke, but the association plateaued and showed no additional benefit beyond moderate intake (~3 servings/week), and confidence was limited by heterogeneous study quality (heart.bmj.com/content/105/1/49). Another meta-analysis of prospective studies similarly reported a modest inverse association between chocolate intake and stroke/CHD risk, but authors noted inconsistency across studies (mdpi.com/2072-6643/9/7/688). Most underlying data come from observational cohorts (e.g., Neurology, 2012) that are prone to confounding—chocolate eaters may have different socioeconomic status, diet, and health behaviors—and reverse causation cannot be ruled out.

**Mechanistic plausibility:** Cocoa flavanols do have real, RCT-demonstrated effects on endothelial function, nitric oxide production, and blood pressure (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S027869152100154X; academic.oup.com/eurjpc/article/32/14/1322/8092214), giving biological plausibility to a protective effect—though these are surrogate markers, not hard stroke outcomes.

**Stronger causal evidence:** A Mendelian randomization study, designed to reduce confounding, found genetically-predicted higher dark chocolate intake associated with reduced hypertension/cardiovascular disease risk (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10781976/), lending some support to a real, modest protective effect.

**Conclusion:** The claim is likely partially true but overstated—dark chocolate in moderation is associated with modestly lower stroke risk, supported by both observational and some causal (MR) evidence plus plausible mechanisms, but effect sizes are small and benefits don't scale with more chocolate. Calling it entirely "false" overstates the counter-case.
